title: Why Is a Marathon 26.2 Miles?
parts: Quick question. How long is a marathon?
Twenty-six point two miles. About forty-two kilometers.
That is a strange number. Not twenty-five. Not thirty. Not a nice round forty.
Someone had to pick it. And a popular story about the starting line is, according to Olympedia, certainly false.
So why is a marathon twenty-six point two miles?
Let's start with the legend. A Greek messenger runs from the town of Marathon to Athens with news of a victory, and then dies. Or so the story goes.
The legend still gave a French scholar an idea: a race like that for the first modern Olympics, in Athens, in eighteen ninety-six.
That first marathon ran from the town of Marathon to Athens. About forty kilometers, or twenty-five miles.
So was it always twenty-six point two? Not even close.
At the early Olympics, the distance changed from Games to Games, depending on which two points the organizers picked.
Paris, in nineteen hundred, a little over forty kilometers. Saint Louis, in nineteen oh four, about forty. There was no standard. Each race was just a long run from here to there.
Then came London, in July of nineteen oh eight.
The organizers wanted the race to start at Windsor Castle and finish in front of the royal box at the stadium. A princess gave the signal, and the runners were off.
The route came to about twenty-six miles, plus three hundred eighty-five yards on the stadium track.
Why those yards? One account says the royal entrance could not be used, so the organizers picked another entrance and reversed the direction around the track.
That cut the lap inside the stadium down to three hundred eighty-five yards.
Now the famous story. It says the royal family wanted the race to start under the nursery windows, so the royal children could watch.
Olympedia says that story is certainly false.

Newspaper notices from the year before show the organizers were asking permission to start at Windsor. The royal family had not asked. So the nursery window is a nice story, but the records do not back it up.
What really happened that day was better than the myth.
An Italian runner, Dorando Pietri, took the lead about a mile from the finish.
He staggered into the stadium, exhausted. He fell, got up, and fell again.
Officials helped him to his feet and across the line.
The Americans protested, and Pietri was disqualified. Johnny Hayes, of the United States, got the gold medal.
The next day, Queen Alexandra gave Pietri a special cup. He became a celebrity anyway.
In nineteen twenty-one, the international athletics federation made twenty-six miles and three hundred eighty-five yards the official marathon distance.
Its own minutes are reportedly silent on why. So we know who made it official, but not exactly why.
The Olympics have used it every time since nineteen twenty-four.
Now the practical part, if you run, or if you are going to watch one.
Official courses are measured along the shortest possible route a runner could take. Hugging every inside curve, across the whole width of the road.
In a real race, nobody runs that perfect line, especially in a crowd.
So your watch will probably read a little long. That is often not a mistake. It is extra distance you actually ran.
People who measure courses also add a small safety margin, about a tenth of a percent, so a course is never short. If you run, trust the course markers for the official distance.
If you are watching, the stretch after the twenty-six-mile mark is roughly those three hundred eighty-five yards. Save some cheering for it.
So the most famous number in running is, more or less, a leftover from one London race.
Which makes you wonder about the other numbers nobody explains. What everyday number is really just a leftover from one day long ago?
